'''Eunice Macaulay''' (''nee'' '''Eunice Bagley''') (July 5, 1923 – July 8, 2013) was a British-born Academy Award–winning animator whose credits range from animation to writing, directing, and producing.

==Biography==
Eunice Bagley was born in [[St Helens, Merseyside|St Helens]] in Lancashire, England.<ref name=IMDb/> Her first job was as a trainee chemist at [[Pilkington Brothers]].<ref name=TCE/> During World War II, she  served in the [[Women's Royal Naval Service]] as a radio mechanic. In the 1950s, she became a graphic artist and greeting card designer.<ref name=obit/> She shifted into animation when a Christmas card she had designed got her a job with Gaumont British Animation (later part of the [[Rank Organisation]]) in 1948.<ref name=TCE/> Starting out as a [[inker|tracer]], she went on to hold nearly every position in animation, including background artist, ink and paint supervisor, rendering supervisor, writer, animator, producer, and director.<ref name=TCE/>

In the early 1960s, Macaulay and her filmmaker husband, Jim Macaulay emigrated to the United States.<ref name=TCE/> She worked as a freelancer in both the United States and Canada.<ref name=TCE/> In 1969, she took a job with [[Potterton Productions]], and in 1973 she was hired full-time by the [[National Film Board of Canada]] (NFB).<ref name=TCE/>

She worked on 25 films altogether, including 18 as artist or animator, 10 as producer, 5 as writer, and 1 as director. She won many awards, including the [[Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film]] for the 1978 film ''[[Special Delivery (1978 film)|Special Delivery]]'', which she cowrote and directed with John Weldon.<ref name=TCE/>  It also took first prize at [[Animafest Zagreb]].<ref name=Lenburg/> Funded by the NFB, it is a dryly humorous account of what happened after a mailman's unexpected death.<ref name=Lenburg/> It was released in both English and in a French-language version.

She served as the producer on the animated short ''[[George and Rosemary]]'' (1987), which was nominated for an Oscar, and on ''Just for Kids'' (1983), a series of adaptations of children's stories by Canadian writers.<ref name=TCE/> Other credits include writer on [[Ishu Patel]]'s ''[[Paradise (1984 film)|Paradise]]'', which was nominated for an Oscar in 1985, and writer/producer on Robert Doucet's ''Dreams of a Land'' (1987), about [[Samuel de Champlain]].<ref name=TCE/>

She retired from the NFB in 1990 and died in [[Hawkesbury, Ontario]].<ref name=IMDb/><ref name=TCE/>

==Personal life==
She was married to Jim Macaulay. She had two daughters, Lesley and Maggi.<ref name=obit/>
